_comment: One story is an ordered list of pages. Each page is one illustration and one spoken line; the owl turns the page when the line finishes. A page's `audio` is a filename in audio/ — when it is absent or the file is missing, the owl speaks the text with the synthesiser instead, so a half-recorded pack still plays.
_gap: The brief asks for at least six stories per hero. One per hero is here, enough to build and test Stories mode. The rest is writing, not engineering.

pages.text: One frosty morning, Fern the Fox found a little red mitten lying in the snow.
It was much too small for her paw. Someone with very small hands must be very cold.
So Fern set off through the quiet wood, holding the mitten carefully in her teeth.
She asked the sleepy owl, and the owl said, try the little house under the roots.
There sat a small mouse with one bare paw tucked under her chin.
Fern gave back the mitten. The mouse smiled, and the whole wood felt a little warmer.
Pip the Bunny was the smallest bunny in the whole meadow.
The grass grew so tall that Pip could never see where he was going.
He tried jumping. He tried standing on a stone. He still could not see.
So Pip stopped trying to see over the grass, and looked at what was inside it.
Down there he found beetles, and clover, and a tiny path only he could fit through.
Being small, Pip decided, was not so bad after all.
Bramble the Bear loved honey more than anything in the world.
He found a jar on a high shelf and tipped it right over his paw.
But honey does not hurry. It moved slower than a snail on a cold day.
Bramble huffed. Bramble sighed. Bramble sat down to wait.
And while he waited, he watched the sun come through the window and the dust dance in it.
When the honey finally came, it was the sweetest thing he had ever tasted.
Tilly the Mouse did not like the dark corner behind the cupboard.
Every night she ran past it very fast with her eyes shut tight.
One night she heard a small sound from the corner. A very small sound.
Tilly took one step closer. Then another. Then she opened her eyes.
It was only a beetle, lost, looking for the way home.
Tilly showed him the way. After that, the corner was just a corner.
Nub the Hedgehog lived under the garden hedge, all by himself.
When anybody came near, Nub rolled into a ball and waited for them to go.
One evening a small voice said hello, and then it sat down and waited too.
It waited a long while. Longer than anyone had ever waited for Nub.
So Nub uncurled, just a little, and looked with one eye.
And there was a friend, who had been there the whole time.
